title: Advanced trigonometry
blurb: Radians, any angle, the sine and cosine rules, compound angles, and trig equations.

rad.name: Radians and arc length
rad.phrase: π is 180°. To radians, × π/180. To degrees, × 180/π.
rad.also: Arc = radius × angle: s = rθ, with θ in radians.
steps: Remember one fact: π radians = 180°.
Degrees to radians: multiply by π/180. 60° = 60π/180 = π/3.
Radians to degrees: swap π for 180°. 3π/4 = 3 × 180° ÷ 4 = 135°.
Arc length s = rθ and sector area = ½r²θ, with θ in radians.
rad.exception: s = rθ only works with θ in radians. Check your calculator mode: sin 30 in radian mode is not 1/2. One radian is about 57.3°, not 1°.

allied.name: Allied angles
allied.phrase: Odd multiple of 90° swaps sin ↔ cos. ASTC decides the sign.
allied.also: 180° and 360° keep the name. 90° and 270° change it.
steps: Write the angle as 90°, 180°, 270°, or 360° plus or minus θ.
180° or 360° (even multiples of 90°): keep the name.
90° or 270° (odd multiples): swap sin ↔ cos and tan ↔ cot.
Pretend θ is small to see which quadrant you land in.
ASTC gives the sign of the original function in that quadrant.
allied.exception: The sign comes from the original function in the new quadrant, not from the new name. cos(90° + θ) = −sin θ because cos is negative in quadrant II. Also, sin(−θ) = −sin θ but cos(−θ) = cos θ.

sine.name: Sine rule
sine.phrase: Each side over the sine of the angle it faces: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C.
steps: Label: side a faces angle A, b faces B, c faces C.
Use it when you know a side and the angle it faces, plus one more side or angle.
Write the two fractions you need and cross-multiply.
For an angle: sin B = b sin A ÷ a. Then check whether 180° − B also fits.
sine.exception: The ambiguous case: with two sides and an angle that is not between them (SSA), sin B gives two angles, B and 180° − B. Both work if the angles still add to less than 180°. If you know two sides and the angle between them, use the cosine rule instead.

cosine.name: Cosine rule
cosine.phrase: Pythagoras with a correction: a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A.
cosine.also: For an angle, flip it round: cos A = (b² + c² − a²) ÷ 2bc.
steps: Use it for two sides and the angle between them (to find the third side).
Or for three sides (to find an angle).
Side: a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A, then take the root.
Angle: cos A = (b² + c² − a²) ÷ 2bc, then use cos⁻¹.
cosine.exception: A must be the angle between b and c. If A is obtuse, cos A is negative, so the correction adds and a gets longer. At A = 90°, the correction is 0 and it is plain Pythagoras. Work out 2bc cos A before subtracting.

area.name: Area with sine
area.phrase: Half of two sides times the sine of the angle between.
area.also: Area = ½ab sin C. For a parallelogram, drop the half.
steps: Pick two sides that meet at a known angle.
Multiply the two sides.
Multiply by the sine of the angle between them.
Halve it.
area.exception: The angle must be between the two sides you use. An obtuse angle is fine: sin 150° = sin 30° = 1/2. Use sin, not cos.

compound.name: Compound angles
compound.phrase: sin cos cos sin, sign stays. cos cos sin sin, sign swaps.
compound.also: tan(A + B) = (tan A + tan B) ÷ (1 − tan A tan B).
steps: sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B.
cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B.
tan(A ± B) = (tan A ± tan B) ÷ (1 ∓ tan A tan B).
Split an awkward angle into table angles: 75° = 45° + 30°, 15° = 45° − 30°.
compound.exception: sin(A + B) is not sin A + sin B: sin 90° is 1, but sin 60° + sin 30° is about 1.37. In cos the sign flips: cos(A + B) has a minus.

double.name: Double angles
double.phrase: Double the angle: sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A.
double.also: cos 2A has three faces: cos²A − sin²A, 2cos²A − 1, and 1 − 2sin²A.
steps: Put B = A in the compound formulas.
sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A.
cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A.
tan 2A = 2 tan A ÷ (1 − tan²A).
double.exception: sin 2A is not 2 sin A: sin 60° is √3/2, but 2 sin 30° is 1. Pick the cos 2A face that fits what you know: if only sin is given, use 1 − 2sin²A.

equations.name: Solving trig equations
equations.phrase: Find the reference angle, then let ASTC place it.
equations.also: Quadrant I: θ. II: 180° − θ. III: 180° + θ. IV: 360° − θ.
steps: Get the ratio alone, like sin θ = −1/2.
Find the reference angle from the table, ignoring the sign: 30°.
Use ASTC to pick the quadrants where the sign is right: sin negative is III and IV.
equations.exception: Don’t stop at the calculator’s one answer; most equations have two in 0° to 360°. sin θ = 2 has none, because sin and cos stay between −1 and 1. Never divide both sides by sin θ or cos θ; you lose the answers where it is 0. Factor instead.

prove.name: Proving identities
prove.phrase: Work on the messier side; turn everything into sin and cos.
prove.also: Never cross the = sign: reshape one side until it looks like the other.
steps: Pick the messier side.
Rewrite tan, cot, sec, and cosec in sin and cos.
Combine fractions over one bottom.
Use sin² + cos² = 1 to simplify.
Stop when it matches the other side.
prove.exception: Do not move terms across the = sign or do the same thing to both sides; that assumes what you want to prove. Checking one angle is not a proof, but one angle that fails does disprove it.

inverse.name: Inverse trig
inverse.phrase: sin⁻¹ asks: which angle has this sine?
inverse.also: Principal ranges: sin⁻¹ and tan⁻¹ give −90° to 90°. cos⁻¹ gives 0° to 180°.
steps: Read sin⁻¹ x as “the angle whose sine is x”.
Find the reference angle from the table.
Give the one answer in the principal range.
sin⁻¹ and tan⁻¹: negative inputs give negative angles. cos⁻¹: negative inputs give angles from 90° to 180°.
inverse.exception: sin⁻¹x is not 1 ÷ sin x; that is cosec x. sin⁻¹ 2 does not exist, because sine never passes 1. cos⁻¹(−1/2) is 120°, not −60°: cos⁻¹ answers live in 0° to 180°.

sohadv.name: SOHCAHTOA still rules
sohadv.phrase: Even in advanced trig, a right triangle still speaks SOH CAH TOA.
steps: Drop a perpendicular if needed.
Label opp/adj/hyp for the acute angle.
Read the primary ratio.
sohadv.exception: Oblique triangles need sine/cosine rules — not plain SOHCAHTOA alone.

astc2.name: ASTC for allied angles
astc2.phrase: All Students Take Calculus — fix the sign after the allied reduction.
steps: Reduce to a related acute angle.
Ask which quadrant the original angle sits in.
Apply ASTC for the sign.
astc2.exception: Odd multiples of 90° can swap sin ↔ cos — do the swap before the sign.

wordkeys2.name: Ambiguous case words
wordkeys2.phrase: SSA is the ambiguous case — two triangles, one, or none.
steps: Spot two sides and a non-included angle.
Compute the height a sin A.
Compare the opposite side to that height and to a.
wordkeys2.exception: If angle A is obtuse, the “two triangles” story changes — check carefully.

compound2.name: Compound sign memory
compound2.phrase: sin cos cos sin, sign stays. cos cos sin sin, sign swaps.
steps: For sin(A±B): sin A cos B ± cos A sin B (sign stays).
For cos(A±B): cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B (sign swaps).
Write carefully.
compound2.exception: tan compound formulas are different — don’t force this chant onto tan.

double2.name: Double-angle pack
double2.phrase: sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A. cos 2A has three outfits.
steps: Sine double: 2 sin cos.
Cosine double: cos²−sin², or 2cos²−1, or 1−2sin².
Pick the outfit that matches what you know.

arith2.name: Exact-value arithmetic
arith2.phrase: Build bigger angles from 30°, 45°, 60° with compound formulas.
steps: Write the angle as a sum/difference of standards.
Apply compound formulas.
Simplify exact values.
arith2.exception: 75° = 45°+30° works; don’t invent a standard for 20°.

estimate2.name: Bound trig answers
estimate2.phrase: Sine and cosine live between −1 and 1 — reject impossible calculator slips.
steps: Solve the equation.
Check each candidate is in range.
Use ASTC to place angles.
estimate2.exception: tan can be any real number — the −1…1 bound is only for sin/cos (and their reciprocals’ domains).

mental2.name: Mental radians
mental2.phrase: π is 180°. Half is 90°, a third is 60°, a quarter is 45°.
steps: Memorize π ↔ 180°.
Divide π to get the common friends.
Convert by ×180/π or ×π/180.
